title: My Parents Tried to Give My Sister the House I Spent Six Years Buying

author: admin

blocks.text: At my sister Kelsey's engagement barbecue in Dayton, Dad held up a house key and said, "We decided the house Melanie's been buying should go to the one starting a family."
Everyone around the patio laughed. Some of them clapped. A couple of my aunts looked at me with polite smiles, waiting for me to nod along like I usually did.
I didn't nod. I set my paper plate down on the edge of the picnic table and stood up.

The backyard went quiet except for the radio playing softly from the open garage. Dad kept his arm raised for another second, his grin tightening at the corners. Kelsey looked from Dad to me, her brow pulled together.
"What are you talking about?" Kelsey asked. "Dad said your deal was cancelled."
"I've lived there for six years. I put twenty thousand dollars down, and I haven't missed a single monthly payment."

Mom stepped over from the folding table where she'd been setting out brownies. She didn't look at the guests. She reached into her purse, pulled out a folded sheet of white paper, and slid it across the picnic table toward me.
"Just sign it, Melanie," Mom whispered, keeping her voice low enough that Kelsey's fiancé, Tyler, wouldn't hear from the grill. "You're single. You don't need three bedrooms. She needs the space."
I looked down at the paper. It was a homemade-looking mutual cancellation agreement printed off some website, with a blank line for my signature at the bottom. I didn't touch it with my fingers.
I used the back of my knuckle to push it back across the wood toward her.
Dad let out a short breath, almost a chuckle, and looked over at Tyler. "Relax," Dad said loudly. "Our names are still on the deed."

A few people laughed again, nervous this time, trying to smooth over the sudden stiffness in the yard. Tyler gave a tight smile and flipped a burger on the grill. Kelsey stared at the paper sitting in front of Mom, her mouth slightly open.

I picked up my purse from the bench, told Kelsey congratulations, and walked through the side gate to my car. My hands were shaking so hard on the steering wheel that I sat in the driveway for two minutes before I could put the car in reverse.
I'm fifty-four years old. I've worked in medical billing at the same clinic outside Dayton for nineteen years.
I never married, and I never had kids, which in my family meant my time, my money, and my plans were always treated like placeholders until someone else needed them.

Six years ago, my parents owned a small brick ranch house on Elmwood Avenue that they'd inherited from my grandmother. It had sat empty for eight months because they didn't want the hassle of being landlords, and the roof was starting to leak. I had been renting a cramped duplex across town, saving every spare dollar I could. Dad offered to sell me the house on a land installment contract.

We didn't just shake hands on it. I insisted on doing it right. I paid for a real estate attorney in Kettering to draw up the contract, and we went down to the Montgomery County Recorder's Office together to have it officially recorded.
I gave them $20,000 from my savings as a down payment.

Under the contract, I was paying $850 a month for ten years at four percent interest, plus all property taxes, homeowner's insurance, and repairs. Once the final payment cleared, the deed would transfer to my name.

Over those six years, I put a new roof on that house. I replaced the furnace when it died in January three years ago. I stripped the peeling wallpaper in the bedrooms, painted every wall myself, and paid the county treasurer every six months without fail.
And every month, on the first, I wrote a check for $850 to my father and dropped it in the mail, or handed it to him when I stopped by on Sundays.
When I got home from the barbecue that afternoon, I didn't even take off my shoes.
I went straight to the spare bedroom where I keep my filing cabinet, pulled out the bottom drawer, and lifted out the thick manila folder labeled Elmwood Contract.
Inside was my certified copy of the recorded land installment contract, stamped by the Montgomery County Recorder. Next to it was my payment ledger and photocopies of my cashed checks.
I sat at my kitchen table with my reading glasses on and checked every single date. Seventy-two months. Seventy-two checks. Every single one cleared Dad's bank account.
Then I noticed something I hadn't paid attention to before.

Usually, Dad deposited my check within two or three days of getting it. When I flipped through the bank printouts from the last four months, the endorsements on the back of the checks looked different. The earlier checks had Dad's messy signature and his personal account number stamped underneath.
The last four checks had a different endorsement stamp.
It wasn't Dad's personal checking account. It was a business account name I didn't recognize: K&T Home Ventures LLC.
My stomach dropped. Dad hadn't just decided to hand over my house at a barbecue. He had been handing my mortgage checks straight to my sister and her fiancé for the last four months.

I didn't call my parents that night. If I called while I was angry, Mom would cry and Dad would talk over me until I started apologizing just to stop the noise. That was how it had worked my whole life.
Instead, I took a personal day from the clinic on Monday morning.
By nine o'clock, I was sitting across from Garrett Vance, the same real estate attorney in Kettering who had drafted my land contract six years earlier.
Garrett pulled my file and looked over the certified copy I'd brought, along with the bank printouts showing the endorsements.

"Your father is right about one thing," Garrett said, tapping the front page of the contract. "His and your mother's names are still on the legal title until the contract is paid in full. That's how a land installment contract works in Ohio."
"So can he just give it to my sister?" I asked.

"No," Garrett said flatly. "Because this contract is properly executed and recorded with the county, you hold equitable title. He cannot legally transfer clear title to your sister, he cannot evict you without a formal foreclosure process, and he certainly cannot cancel a recorded contract unilaterally.
That paper your mother tried to get you to sign at the barbecue was an attempt to get you to surrender your rights voluntarily."
I let out a breath I felt like I'd been holding since Saturday afternoon. "What about the checks? Why are they going into my sister's LLC?"

"A seller can assign their right to receive payments, though usually they have to notify you," Garrett said. "More importantly, if he's depositing them into a third-party account, you need a complete paper trail showing every dollar went toward your principal and interest under the contract. We should also pull a current title search on the property right now, just to make sure your father hasn't taken out any new loans or liens against the deed."
I paid Garrett's retainer on my credit card and asked him to run the title search immediately.
It was Kelsey. I let it go to voicemail, pulled into a grocery store parking lot, and listened to the message.

"Mel, please call me back," Kelsey said, sounding breathless and annoyed. "Mom and Dad are furious, and Tyler is really stressed out. Can we just meet for coffee and talk like adults? You're making this way bigger than it needs to be."
I didn't call her back, but I texted her: I can meet at the Panera on Far Hills at 5:30. Just you.

Kelsey showed up ten minutes late, wearing her scrubs from the dental office where she worked as a hygienist. She sat down across from me without getting anything to drink and folded her arms on the table.
"Look," she said before I could even speak. "I honestly didn't know you were still under contract.
Dad told me back in February that you were tired of the upkeep and wanted out, and that he was letting me and Tyler take over the house as an engagement gift."
I stared at her. "Kelsey, you came to my house for Easter in April. You saw the new mulch I put down. You helped me hang curtains in the dining room. Did I sound like someone moving out?"

Kelsey shifted in her seat and looked down at her hands. "I thought maybe you were just fixing it up before leaving. Whatever. The point is, Tyler and I already told his parents we're moving in after the wedding in October. Our apartment lease ends in September."
"That's between you and Dad," I said. "I've paid twenty thousand down and over sixty-one thousand in monthly payments. Where did you think I was going to live?"

"Mom said you have a good job and retirement savings. She said you could easily get a nice one-bedroom condo near the clinic, and Dad offered to give you back part of your down payment once Tyler and I refinance the house in our names."
"Refinance it," I repeated. "With what?"

Kelsey paused. Her cheeks turned pink. "Tyler's credit isn't great right now because of his landscaping business startup, so we needed equity to qualify for a construction loan to add a sunroom and redo the kitchen. Dad said since the Elmwood house is worth almost two hundred and forty thousand now, we could use that equity."
Everything clicked into place with a dull ache behind my eyes.
When I bought the house from my parents six years ago, it was worth $115,000. That was the exact purchase price on my contract.

Over the last six years, Dayton property values had climbed, and I had put twenty-five thousand dollars of my own money into the roof, furnace, siding, and floors. Now the house was worth more than double what I owed on it.

Dad hadn't given Kelsey the house out of the goodness of his heart. He was trying to hand her $125,000 in equity that I had built, using my house as collateral for Tyler's business and their wedding plans.
"And what about my checks?" I asked quietly. "The last four months were endorsed to K&T Home Ventures."
